title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite and full of stars, why isn't the whole sky as bright as the sun?
summary: A seemingly childish question about the dark night sky turns out to require the Big Bang, the finite age of the universe, and the finite speed of light to answer.
content:
Stand outside on a clear night and look up. Most of the sky is black, dotted with a few thousand visible points of light. This seems obvious and unremarkable—until you ask why. If the universe is infinite, eternal, and roughly uniformly filled with stars, then every single line of sight you could draw from your eye should eventually terminate on the surface of a star. The whole sky should blaze like a sun, night and day. It doesn't. That gap between expectation and observation is Olbers' Paradox, named for the 19th-century astronomer who popularized it, though Kepler and others had wrestled with versions of it centuries earlier.

The Naive Argument

Imagine the universe as a uniform, infinite forest of trees (stars). Even though trees far away look smaller and dimmer individually, the number of trees at a given distance grows with the surface area of a sphere at that distance—proportional to the square of the distance. But brightness falls off as the inverse square of distance. Those two effects exactly cancel. So every "shell" of space at any distance from Earth contributes the same total brightness. Add up infinitely many shells, and you get infinite light. Eventually every sightline should hit a stellar surface, the way every sightline into a sufficiently dense infinite forest eventually hits a tree trunk.

Why the Universe Isn't Actually a Blaze of Light

The resolution isn't a single clever trick; it's that two of the paradox's premises are false. First, the universe is not infinitely old. It is about 13.8 billion years old, and light travels at a finite speed, so we can only ever see stars whose light has had time to reach us—a finite "observable universe." Sightlines that would terminate on a star ten trillion light-years away simply haven't caught up to us yet, and may never will if the universe's expansion outpaces the journey.

Second, even for the stars whose light does reach us, most of it arrives enormously redshifted and diluted by the expansion of space, and stars themselves don't live forever—they burn out, so the "shells" far enough away in time correspond to an era before most stars had even formed. The night sky is dark not because starlight can't reach us in principle, but because the universe has a beginning, a finite light-travel budget, and a history in which light-emitting matter appeared only after some cosmic dawn.

The Universe Isn't Silent, Either

In a real sense, the "glow" the naive argument predicted does exist—it's just not visible light anymore. The afterglow of the hot early universe, stretched by billions of years of cosmic expansion, now arrives as the cosmic microwave background: a nearly uniform bath of microwave radiation filling every direction of the sky at about 2.7 kelvin. If you could see microwaves, the whole sky genuinely would glow, faintly and uniformly, exactly as the paradox's logic demanded—just redshifted into a wavelength human eyes can't register. Olbers wasn't wrong that something should fill the sky; he was only missing that "something" had cooled and stretched into invisibility.

A Question That Outlived Its Answer

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable is how much cosmology it forces into view from an observation any child could make. To explain a dark sky, you need a universe with a finite age, a finite speed of light, an evolving population of stars, and space itself expanding and cooling radiation over time. A question phrased in 1610 anticipated evidence that wouldn't exist until the 20th century. It's a reminder that "obvious" observations can be probes into the deepest structure of reality, if you're willing to ask why they're obvious.

perspectives.title: Historical Astronomy Perspective
perspectives.description: Thomas Digges, Kepler, Halley, Cheseux, and Olbers each grappled with versions of this puzzle across three centuries, each proposing partial explanations (absorbing dust, finite star fields) that later turned out to be incomplete or wrong.

perspectives.title: Cosmological Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox is resolved by the universe's finite age and the finite speed of light, which cap how much starlight can possibly have reached any observer, regardless of how large or infinite space itself is.

perspectives.title: Astrophysical Perspective
perspectives.description: Stars have finite lifespans and formed only after the universe cooled enough for structure to condense, so much of cosmic history contains no starlight sources at all to contribute to the night sky's brightness.

perspectives.title: Physics of Light Perspective
perspectives.description: Cosmological redshift dilutes and stretches distant light into longer wavelengths and lower energy, so even light that does arrive from the deep past contributes far less visible brightness than naive geometry predicts.

openQuestions: If the universe's expansion accelerates forever, will more of the sky recede beyond any possible observation, making the night sky effectively darker over cosmic time?
What would the night sky look like to an observer in a universe with different physical constants or a different age?
Could an infinite universe with a non-uniform, fractal distribution of matter avoid the paradox without needing a finite age at all?
How much of what feels 'obvious' in everyday experience is actually encoding deep facts about the universe's history that we haven't thought to question yet?
